name: Desktop Computer
blurb: A typical office desktop draws 100–200 watts in use, more under load. Left running around the clock, an ordinary PC can cost more per year than a refrigerator — sleep settings are the single biggest lever.
tips: Set sleep after 15–20 minutes idle; modern PCs wake in seconds.
Skip screensavers — they keep the GPU and monitor fully powered.
If it must stay on for remote access, enable wake-on-LAN and let it sleep anyway.

name: Gaming PC
blurb: A gaming rig with a serious GPU pulls 300–800 watts during play — several times a console. Four hours a day of AAA gaming is a real line item on the bill, comparable to running a window AC unit the same hours.
tips: Cap frame rates to your monitor's refresh — uncapped menus can burn maximum wattage rendering frames you never see.
Enable GPU power-saving for non-gaming use; browsing shouldn't cost 400 watts.
Undervolting modern CPUs/GPUs often cuts 10–20% of power at nearly identical performance.

name: Laptop
blurb: Laptops are dramatically cheaper to run than desktops, averaging 30–60 watts in use. A full workday of laptop computing costs a few cents — for most people the monitor plugged into it uses a comparable amount.

name: Computer Monitor
blurb: A 24–27 inch LED monitor draws 20–40 watts; big ultrawides and bright HDR panels push 60+. Auto-sleep on idle matters more than size — a monitor glowing at a lock screen all night wastes more than your workday used.

name: Wi-Fi Router
blurb: Routers run 24/7 at 6–20 watts. That constant draw lands around a dollar or two per month in most states — worth knowing, but not worth the connectivity headaches of switching it off at night.

name: Cable Modem
blurb: A cable or fiber modem adds another 6–15 always-on watts alongside the router. Combined home networking gear typically totals 20–40 watts of permanent draw — a small but genuinely constant bill floor.

name: Mesh Wi-Fi Node
blurb: Each mesh satellite adds 5–15 watts of continuous draw, so a three-node system roughly triples the router line on your bill. Place nodes well rather than adding more of them.

name: NAS (Network Storage)
blurb: A two-to-four-bay NAS idles at 20–40 watts with drives spun down and more under load, around the clock. Enabling scheduled disk hibernation is the main way to keep a home NAS from costing more than the cloud storage it replaced.

name: Home Server / Homelab
blurb: Repurposed desktops and rack servers running 24/7 at 40–300 watts are the classic homelab surprise: a single old Xeon box can add hundreds of dollars a year. Idle efficiency — not peak specs — is what a home server's cost is made of.

name: Printer
blurb: Inkjets sip power, while laser printers spike to several hundred watts during fusing — but only for seconds per page. For home volumes, standby draw over weeks typically exceeds the printing itself.

name: 3D Printer
blurb: A consumer FDM printer averages 50–150 watts once the bed is heated, so a typical multi-hour print uses roughly half a kilowatt-hour. Even heavy hobby printing usually costs less per month than a single spool of filament.

name: Phone Charger
blurb: Charging a smartphone every night uses roughly 5–10 kWh per year — about a dollar or two annually in most states. The charger left plugged in without a phone draws almost nothing on modern hardware.

name: Tablet Charger
blurb: Tablets hold two to three times a phone's battery, but yearly charging still totals only a few dollars. Battery devices in general are rounding errors next to anything that heats or cools.

name: Security Camera (Wired)
blurb: Each wired security camera draws 3–10 watts continuously, with infrared night vision at the upper end. A six-camera system plus its recorder can quietly total 50+ always-on watts — worth counting in a standby audit.

name: Video Doorbell
blurb: Hardwired video doorbells trickle 2–6 watts around the clock. Annual cost lands around a dollar or two — the subscription costs far more than the electricity.

name: Baby Monitor
blurb: Camera-based baby monitors draw 3–10 watts across the camera and parent unit. Overnight use every night still totals under a dollar a month nearly everywhere.

name: UPS Battery Backup
blurb: A UPS consumes 5–40 watts of overhead keeping its battery charged and electronics ready — before counting the equipment plugged into it. Oversized units carry proportionally larger idle losses.

name: Starlink Dish
blurb: A Starlink terminal draws a steady 40–75 watts including its router — several times typical wired-internet gear. Running around the clock, it's often the largest single always-on electronics load in an off-grid or rural home.

name: Crypto Mining Rig
blurb: A mining rig is a space heater that computes: 600–3,000 watts, 24 hours a day. Electricity is the dominant cost of mining, and profitability swings entirely on your state's rate — the spread between the cheapest and most expensive states is nearly 4×.
